title: Pakistan Calls NYT Report of Its Jets Striking Houthis 'Fake and Fabricated'
excerpt: Islamabad denied that its air force flew strike missions against the Houthis even as the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact faces its first test in the escalating Yemen war.
body:
• The New York Times reported that Pakistani fighter jets carried out strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen, citing a senior Pakistani military official who described it as air support to counter drone and missile threats.
  • Pakistan's information ministry flatly rejected the report as "fake and fabricated," urging international media to avoid speculative reporting on its military's role under the Makkah joint defence agreement.
  • The dispute sits inside a rapidly escalating regional war: Saudi Arabia signed a joint defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan last month, both countries are sending troops and equipment to the kingdom, and the US and Britain are assisting Saudi airstrikes with intelligence and refuelling.
  • India is watching closely — nearly 2.5 million Indians live in Saudi Arabia and the region's air and shipping lanes are vital to Indian trade and travel.

Pakistan has rejected a New York Times report that its air force fighter jets were used in strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen, calling the claim "fake and fabricated" even as the kingdom's war against the Iran-aligned group draws in a widening circle of regional powers.

The Times reported that Pakistani jets had carried out strikes against the Houthis, citing a senior Pakistani military official who described the operation as air support to counter Houthi drone and missile threats, and ruled out any Pakistani ground offensive inside Yemen. A second official confirmed the air-support framing. In response, the fact-check account of Pakistan's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting posted on X that the story was fabricated, urged "international media organisations to avoid speculative reporting with regard to the employment of Pakistan's Military Forces under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement," and said any details of military employment would come from the concerned authorities.

The Mecca Pact in action

"India is watching closely — nearly 2.5 million Indians live in Saudi Arabia and the region's air and shipping lanes are vital to Indian trade and travel."

The dispute lands at the first real test of the joint defence agreement Saudi Arabia signed with Turkey and Pakistan last month — informally called the Mecca Pact — which commits each country to come to the others' defence. Pakistan's defence minister has said an attack on Saudi Arabia could activate the agreement, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

Whether or not Pakistani jets have flown strike missions, Islamabad's military footprint around the conflict is already substantial. Pakistan has flown cargo planes of military equipment — including air defence systems, light artillery, drones and anti-drone systems — to Aden in southern Yemen, deployed troops inside Saudi Arabia to help defend its borders, and stationed military advisers alongside Saudi counterparts, according to Pakistani and regional officials. Turkey, which still needs to ratify the pact internally, said it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom, including military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.

A widening war

The Saudi-led offensive aims to retake the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the vital Red Sea shipping lane the Houthis seized last month, and reverse the group's territorial gains. Saudi-backed forces have launched a counterattack around the strait, while the Houthis have simultaneously advanced inland, surrounding the city of Taiz. The United States and Britain are assisting the Saudi airstrikes with intelligence on Houthi targets and jet refuelling. Syria has also said it would consider military cooperation with Riyadh.

The Houthis have answered by striking deep into Saudi territory — attacks on the airports in Riyadh and Abha this week killed three people, prompted Lufthansa and Indian carriers to suspend Riyadh flights, and drew a safety advisory from the Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia.

Why it matters for India

New Delhi has stayed publicly neutral, but the stakes are direct. Nearly 2.5 million Indians live in Saudi Arabia, Indian shipping moves through the Bab al-Mandeb, and any disruption to Gulf aviation and oil flows lands on Indian consumers and travellers. Pakistan's deepening military role in a Saudi-led war — and Islamabad's sensitivity about how it is reported — also complicates India's own diplomacy with both Riyadh and Islamabad at a moment of already high tension.

What to watch

The question now is whether Pakistan acknowledges a combat role or keeps its involvement confined to equipment, advisers and border defence. A formal Pakistani admission of airstrikes would mark a significant escalation in the country's military posture and invite retaliation threats from the Houthis. Watch for the Saudi government, which has not commented on the NYT report, to clarify the coalition's composition — and for whether Turkey's promised support stays defensive or grows.
